extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (introductory real analysis / advanced calculus)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and standard examples about equivalence relations, cardinality, ordered sets, fields, supremum/infimum, construction/properties of the real numbers, and related exercises for beginning real-analysis students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation and equivalence classes (Proposition 0.3.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is an equivalence relation on a set A, then every a in A is in exactly one equivalence class. Moreover, a R b if and only if [a] = [b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. Exercises ask to prove this and to verify that particular relations (e.g., the relation in Example 0.3.25 for rational construction) are equivalence relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of rationals as equivalence classes (Example 0.3.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of rational numbers can be defined as equivalence classes of pairs (a,b) with a ∈ Z, b ∈ N, where (a,b) ∼ (c,d) whenever ad = bc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Left as an exercise to prove ∼ is an equivalence relation; notation (a/b) is used for the equivalence class. Illustrates how equivalence-class constructions produce familiar number systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality via bijection (Definition 0.3.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality when there exists a bijection f : A → B. Denote |A| for the cardinality of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that 'having the same cardinality' is an equivalence relation: identity shows reflexivity, inverses show symmetry, compositions show transitivity. Notes that bijection to the empty set forces a set to be empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite vs infinite sets and notation (Definition 0.3.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is finite if there exists a bijection between A and {1,2,…,n} for some n ∈ N; otherwise A is infinite. If A is empty write |A| = 0. If A has same cardinality as N, write |A| = ℵ₀ and call it countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification that the natural-number label n is unique is left as an exercise. Exercises explore uniqueness and related properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing cardinalities using injections (Definition 0.3.28)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write |A| ≤ |B| if there exists an injection from A to B. Write |A| < |B| if |A| ≤ |B| but A and B do not have the same cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States (without proof) the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem: A and B have the same cardinality iff injections exist both ways. Notes subtle issues around these statements and omits proofs as not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable and uncountable (Definition 0.3.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if A ≃ N. A is countable if it is finite or countably infinite. If A is not countable it is uncountable. The cardinality of N is denoted ℵ₀.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (even numbers, N×N, Q) to illustrate countability. Exercises cover consequences: subsets of countable sets, unions, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples/proofs of countability (Examples 0.3.30–0.3.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete bijections: even naturals ↔ N via f(n)=2n; N×N is countable via diagonal argument; Q is countable by enumerating rationals and omitting duplicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches and informal enumerations are given; students are prompted to formalize these constructions in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set and its cardinality (Definition 0.3.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: P(A) denotes the power set of A, the set of all subsets of A. For a finite set A of cardinality n, |P(A)| = 2^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include proving the finite case. Notes that for finite A, |P(A)| is strictly larger than |A|, motivating Cantor's theorem for infinite sets as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem: no surjection A → P(A) (Theorem 0.3.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, there is no surjection from A onto P(A); in particular |A| < |P(A)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the diagonal set B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ g(x)} to show any proposed g misses B. Consequences: existence of uncountable sets, and progressively larger infinities via repeated power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered set: trichotomy and transitivity (Definition 1.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered set S has a relation < such that (i) trichotomy: for all x,y∈S exactly one of x<y, x=y, y<x holds; (ii) transitivity: if x<y and y<z then x<z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines ≤, ≥, >; examples include Q, N, Z, lexicographic order on words. Notes relevance in computer science and other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper bounds, lower bounds, supremum and infimum (Definition 1.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: b is an upper bound of E⊂S if x≤b for all x∈E. b₀ is the least upper bound (sup E) if it is an upper bound and b₀ ≤ b for every upper bound b. Analogous definition for infimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks that sup/inf (if they exist) are unique. Examples show supremum need not lie in the set. Figure 1.1 illustrates these ideas. Exercises ask to prove uniqueness and properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Least-upper-bound property / completeness (Definition 1.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered set S has the least-upper-bound property (Dedekind completeness) if every nonempty subset E⊂S that is bounded above has a least upper bound in S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the crucial completeness property of R; Q does not have it (example: {x∈Q: x^2<2} has no supremum in Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field axioms (Definition 1.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A field F is a set with two operations + and · satisfying axioms (A1–A5) for addition, (M1–M5) for multiplication, and distributivity (D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Q is a field; Z is not because multiplicative inverses generally do not exist. Readers are expected to use basic consequences of the axioms (e.g., 0·x = 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered field (Definition 1.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A field F is an ordered field if it is an ordered set and addition and multiplication preserve order: x<y ⇒ x+z<y+z and x>0,y>0 ⇒ xy>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines positive, negative, nonnegative, nonpositive. The rational numbers with standard ordering form an ordered field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary properties of ordered fields (Proposition 1.1.8 & 1.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of standard facts: (i) x>0 ⇒ −x<0; (ii) x>0 and y<z ⇒ xy<xz; (iii) x<0 and y<z ⇒ xy>xz; (iv) x≠0 ⇒ x^2>0; (v) 0<x<y ⇒ 1/y < 1/x; (vi) 0<x<y ⇒ x^2<y^2; (vii) x≤y and z≤w ⇒ x+z ≤ y+w. Also: if xy>0 then x and y have same sign (both positive or both negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs are sketched or left as exercises; these are the routine algebra/order manipulations used throughout analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence/uniqueness of the real numbers (Theorem 1.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a unique (up to isomorphism) ordered field R with the least-upper-bound property that contains Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text assumes existence rather than constructing R explicitly; references (e.g., Rudin) are given for constructions. Many subsequent results depend on this completeness axiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-criterion for smallness (Proposition 1.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x∈R satisfies x ≤ ε for every ε>0 then x ≤ 0 (and in common usage: if x ≤ ε for all ε>0 and x ≥ 0 then x = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the analysts' standard method of proving equality by showing two inequalities via arbitrary ε>0. Connects to absolute-value characterizations in §1.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of square roots and nth roots (Example 1.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a unique positive r∈R with r^2 = 2 (denoted √2); more generally for each x>0 and n∈N there exists a unique positive real r with r^n = x (exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses supremum of the set {x∈R: x^2 < 2} and shows r^2=2 by epsilon-style arguments; uniqueness by monotonicity of squaring on positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean property and density of Q (Theorem 1.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Archimedean: For x,y∈R with x>0 there exists n∈N with n x > y. (ii) Density: If x<y in R then ∃ r∈Q with x<r<y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of (i) uses that N is not bounded above; (ii) follows from (i) via finding n with n(y−x)>1 and choosing appropriate integer m to produce rational m/n between x and y. Corollary: inf {1/n : n∈N} = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic behavior of suprema and infima (Propositions 1.2.6 & 1.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A⊂R nonempty: sup(x + A) = x + sup A; inf(x + A) = x + inf A. If x>0 then sup(xA) = x sup A and inf(xA) = x inf A; if x<0 the roles of sup and inf swap. If x≤y for all x∈A and y∈B then sup A ≤ inf B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs are straightforward manipulations of bounds. Warning: strict inequalities between elements do not necessarily give strict inequality between suprema/infima (example with 1/n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation property of supremum (Proposition 1.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S⊂R is nonempty and bounded above, then for every ε>0 there exists x∈S with sup S − ε < x ≤ sup S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard property used to approximate suprema from below; proof left to reader as routine ε-argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended real numbers and conventions for sup/inf (Definition 1.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions: sup ∅ = −∞, sup of an unbounded-above set = ∞, inf ∅ = ∞, inf of unbounded-below set = −∞. The extended real line R* = R ∪ {−∞, ∞} is ordered with −∞ < x < ∞ for all x∈R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that arithmetic with ±∞ is dangerous (e.g., ∞−∞, 0·∞ undefined) and R* is not a field. These conventions allow talking about sup/inf without checking emptiness or boundedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum and minimum (1.2.4 Maxima and minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bounded set A has sup A ∈ A we call it max A; when inf A ∈ A call it min A. For finite sets, sup and inf exist and lie in the set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: max{1,2.4,π,100}=100, min{1,2.4,π,100}=1. Exercises discuss existence in finite and specially-ordered infinite sets.
